points.point: Broker with a brokerage relationship is responsible for the proper closing; using a title company delegates work, not responsibility
Broker reviews documents and attends or is reasonably available; a firm-designated substitute broker shares responsibility
Closing statement and documents go to the brokerage firm right after closing for the transaction file
Closing Instructions are signed by buyer, seller and closing company; brokers are not parties
Party instructions that conflict with the contract require an Agreement to Amend/Extend signed by buyer and seller
Good funds law: no disbursement until funds are available for immediate withdrawal (wires, cashier's/certified/teller's checks)
Good funds exception: up to $500 may be advanced for incidentals like tax certificates and recording fees
Every transaction, cash or financed, needs a broker-signed closing statement; the federal Closing Disclosure does not replace it
Brokers give copies of every document they prepare to the consumers at the time it is prepared
Colorado is a race-notice state, so the closing company records the deed promptly
Documentary fee: one cent per $100 of consideration, none at $500 or less, collected at recording
Real Property Transfer Declaration (TD-1000) tells the assessor the sale price and is confidential
Contract default: seller selects the title company and pays for the owner's policy; buyer pays the lender's policy
Owner's extended coverage removes standard exceptions such as unrecorded mechanics' liens and survey matters
Title company typically obtains a certificate of taxes due from the county treasurer
Earnest money is a buyer credit, never a seller entry; the price is buyer debit and seller credit
Debit = the party owes it; credit = in the party's favor
Between buyer and seller = double entry; with an outsider = single entry
Paid ahead by the seller = buyer debit/seller credit; paid in arrears = seller debit/buyer credit; rent collected ahead = seller debit/buyer credit
A double entry is the same amount on both sides
Payoffs, commissions and new loans are one-side items with third parties; prorations appear on both sides
Assumed loan is a buyer credit and a seller debit
Colorado property taxes are paid in arrears: a year's taxes are due January 1 of the following year
Unpaid current-year taxes: seller's share is a seller debit and buyer credit
Contract default tax basis is the prior calendar year's taxes with the latest mill levy and valuation; prorations are final
Proration method: daily rate x days, with the buyer owning the closing day in the examples
Rent collected in advance: buyer's days are a seller debit and buyer credit
Security deposits transfer in full (seller debit, buyer credit) and are not prorated
Prepaid HOA dues: seller credit and buyer debit for the buyer's days
Seller requests the association status letter and pays its fee
Documentary fee is figured on the full consideration, not the down payment
Building a statement: buyer's debits minus credits gives cash to close
Proration steps: rate, days, multiply, post
Leasing or managing for others for compensation requires a broker's license; narrow exemption for a salaried on-site apartment/condo manager
A property management firm keeps separate trust accounts for rents and for security deposits
Property management funds are deposited within five business days (earnest money: three)
Owners get regular accountings, generally within 30 days after month end
If the owner holds deposits, the tenant is told in writing who holds them and how to get them back
Maximum residential security deposit is two months' rent
Deposit return: 30 days after lease end or surrender, or up to 60 days if the lease says so
Deductions only for actual cause in reasonable amounts, never for normal wear and tear
No timely written statement of reasons: the landlord forfeits the right to keep any of the deposit
Wrongful retention: treble damages plus attorney fees, after at least 7 days' notice from the tenant
When a rental is sold, deposits are transferred to the new owner with tenant notice, or returned, within 60 days
Warranty of habitability: landlord responds within 24 hours; begins repairs within 24 hours (life/health/safety) or 96 hours (other)
Conditions caused by the tenant, household or guests are not a landlord breach
Eviction demand: 10 days for residential nonpayment or lease violation (5 exempt, 3 nonresidential)
No self-help lockouts or utility shutoffs; tenant recovers damages plus the greater of 3 months' rent or $5,000
For-cause law: after 12 months a landlord generally needs cause or a qualifying no-fault reason to evict or not renew
Brokers use a management agreement and Commission leasing listings (Exclusive Right to Lease for landlords)
Colorado follows prior appropriation, not riparian rights
First to put water to beneficial use holds the senior right; juniors must stop when seniors call
Water rights can be severed and are conveyed with real estate formalities, usually by deed
Mutual ditch company shares are personal property that transfer by stock assignment
Buyer acknowledges the Seller's Property Disclosure or Source of Water Addendum (and well permit copy)
Household-use-only wells allow indoor use in one home; domestic and livestock wells allow more
Exempt well change of ownership: buyer completes the form; closing company files within 60 days
Non-exempt wells on tributary groundwater generally need a water-court-approved augmentation plan
Mineral rights can be severed, creating a split estate with surface-use rights for the mineral owner
Real property is revalued every odd-numbered year based on January 1 classification and use
Tax = actual value x assessment rate x mill levy (mills / 1,000)
Value protests start with the assessor, then the county board of equalization
Documentary fee and TD-1000 travel with the deed (fee at recording; declaration to the assessor)
Special taxing district bold disclosure in every residential contract is the seller's duty
Metro districts organized on/after 2000: seller gives the district's official website
Colorado nonresident withholding: lesser of 2% of price or net proceeds
No withholding at $100,000 or less, with a residency/principal-residence affirmation, or on foreclosure transfers
FIRPTA turns on foreign status; Colorado withholding turns on Colorado residency
Colorado Fair Housing Act adds classes beyond federal law (marital status, creed, sexual orientation, gender identity/expression, ancestry, veteran/military, source of income)
Source of income protects lawful, verifiable income including vouchers
Source-of-income exemption for landlords with three or fewer units; credit checks must apply to everyone
Owners of five or fewer single-family rentals (five units total) may decline federal housing choice vouchers
CCRD charge within one year; private suit within two years
The county public trustee is the trustee under Colorado deeds of trust; most foreclosures are non-judicial
Sale is set 110-125 days after the notice of election and demand is recorded (215-230 agricultural)
Highest bidder receives a certificate of purchase; confirmation deed follows the redemption periods
Cure: notice of intent to cure at least 15 days before sale; pay by noon the day before
No owner redemption after sale; junior lienors redeem, filing notice within 8 business days
Short sale needs lender approval; the Commission's Short Sale Addendum keeps it outside the equity-purchaser rules
Foreclosure consultants may not collect a fee until all services are fully performed
A licensed broker acting within the license is not a foreclosure consultant
Equity purchaser: non-occupant buyer of a principal residence 30+ days delinquent; Commission CFPA contract applies
Homeowner may cancel an equity purchase contract until midnight of the 3rd business day or noon the day before sale, whichever is first
Leaseback, repurchase or loan assumption: CFPA form can't be used; an attorney drafts the contract
Homeowner Warning Notice must be translated if needed, but not by the broker personally
Six-column worksheet: broker (cash) column debit = money in, credit = money out; new loan is buyer credit and cash debit
Earnest money is a buyer credit and cash debit, never a seller entry
Payoff of the seller's loan is a seller debit and cash credit
Double entries move value between buyer and seller with no cash entry (e.g. tax prorations)
Prepaid items the buyer takes over are seller credits; rent collected, accrued items and deposits are seller debits
Single entries involve one party and an outsider plus a cash entry (e.g. brokerage fee)
Assumed loans are double entries (seller debit, buyer credit) with no cash
Seller carry-back notes are double entries (seller debit, buyer credit) with no cash
Seller concessions are double entries: seller debit, buyer credit
Owner's title policy (contract default) is a seller debit and cash credit
Documentary fee: debit whichever party pays it, credit cash
Unpaid prior-year taxes are a full seller debit paid out to the county treasurer
Balance due from buyer is entered as a buyer credit and cash debit
Balance due to seller is entered as a seller debit and cash credit
The cash column must balance; a gap usually means a line is missing its broker entry
The lender's Closing Disclosure doesn't replace the broker-signed Colorado closing statement
Conventions: 365-day year for taxes, buyer owns closing day; seller's tax days are a seller debit
New-loan sale: seller net = credits minus debits, with fee on full price and tax proration as a debit
Accrued interest on an assumed loan (paid in arrears) is a seller debit and buyer credit
The seller's lender escrow reserve on an assumed loan is a seller credit and buyer debit
Assumption sale: buyer's balance due with assumed loan, interest and tax credits
Carry-back sale: the note reduces the seller's cash at closing but the fee is on the full price
Carry-back sale: the note is a buyer credit that reduces the buyer's cash to close
Rental sale: rent for buyer's days plus deposits in full are seller debits
Documentary fee is figured on the full price, not the cash paid
